title: Chapter 81 – The Reagent List
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The Enforcement Hall keeps him for two days, and asks him the same thing forty times.

It is a small bare room with a table and a lamp and a clerk who writes everything down. Deputy Rong sits across from him with his tablet and his gray mustache. He does not raise his voice. He asks about the moonroot and the scale and the register. He asks about the knife, where it came from, who held it, when it was last cleaned. He asks why the boy drew it at the noon weighing and not at the first.

"Because I was not sure," says Jian, for the fortieth time, "until the beam moved."

"Not sure of what?"

"That it was the Deacon's thumb."

"And the pins in the floor?"

"I placed them. I thought a man who rigged a scale might step back from it if he was caught." He keeps his eyes on the lamp. "I am ten, Deputy. I did not think of a Blood Shadow. I thought of a thief."

It is the story he has built from the pieces, and it holds. It holds because most of it is true. Rong writes it down. The lamp burns lower. On the second evening the door opens and Elder Duan comes in and reads the clerk's pages standing, and says to the Deputy, quietly, "He is telling it as he saw it," and goes out again without looking at the boy.

They let him go at the lamp-lighting hour.

He walks back through the Court in the cold blue dusk. The seals have come off the Contribution Hall. The doors stand open. A new Deacon has been installed, a heavy, tired, honest-looking man from the Outer Affairs Hall who sits behind the great scale with his sleeves rolled and says the figures aloud in a voice like a cart on gravel. The real Mo Lian lies in a plain box in the cellar of the Library, under the Arbiter's seal, waiting for a funeral that the Sect has not yet decided how to hold.

It is over, says everyone in the Court. They found it. They cut it out.

It is not over, thinks Jian. The puppet is dead. The hand is not.

He has twenty-four days on the gray line in the corner of his sight. He has no scan, no panel, no blade. He has eleven stones, ninety points, a pangolin, and a plan with five circles on a leaf of cheap paper, and the circle at the top is called Root.

* * *

The mission hall is full when he arrives, because everyone has had the same idea.

Fear has gone out of the Outer Court like a fever. In its place there is a hungry, restless, grateful energy. The disciples have been cooped up for four days under the Hall's seal, and now they pour out and fill the benches of the Outer Affairs Hall and the whitewashed wall of slips with a noise like a market. A servant stands on a stool with a pole, unhooking old tasks and hanging new ones. A line of clerks takes names.

Jian stands in front of the red slips for the third time.

Azure dew. Sun-forged cinnabar. Inner Sect rank. They have not changed. He reads them as one reads a verdict. Then he goes to the left end of the wall, where the medicine missions hang, and finds that the Terrace Eleven slip is gone.

Someone has taken it.

He knows who before he turns.

"I did say I would," says Tan Ruyan, behind him.

She is in a blue-trimmed gray tunic, the tailored one, with the silver comb in her hair. A small leather folder is tucked under her arm. She has been waiting for him, he thinks, and not for long; she waits as she does everything, without appearing to. Beside her, with his hands in his sleeves, stands the tall calm Inner Sect disciple with the jade pin.

"Disciple Lin," she says. "Allow me. This is Senior Brother Wei Chen of the Medicine Valley. He is supervising the expedition."

"Senior Brother."

"Junior." Wei Chen inclines his head a thumb's width. He has the same long calm face Jian remembers from the trial, and the same heavy-lidded eyes, and a voice like a hand laid on a table. "I am told you filed the complaint that brought down a Blood Shadow. I am told it was about moonroot." The corner of his mouth moves. "I should like to hear the story one day. I am sure it is less dull than the official one."

"It is very dull, Senior Brother."

"They always are, when they are true." He gestures at the wall. "The Terrace Eleven harvest has been combined with the Beast Mountains edge mission under a single warrant. The Overseer's valley has lost forty plants this year to beasts, and the Hall wishes to settle the matter at once. A team of four, led by a disciple of the eighth layer or above. A valley harvest and a boar cull. Two weeks, perhaps three." He looks at Tan Ruyan. "Disciple Tan has put her name to the warrant as leader."

"I have," says Tan Ruyan.

"She requires three companions."

Jian says nothing. He is turning the pieces over, very fast. Leader. The marrow goes to the leader. The mission slip said it in so many words. Marrow of a second-rank beast available to the team leader by request. If Tan Ruyan leads the team, the marrow is hers.

"I came to find you," she says. Her smile has not changed. "I find we are in the same line."

"You said we would be civil."

"I did. This is civility." She opens the leather folder. Inside is a single warrant, stamped in blue, with her name in the first column and three blank lines. "I need three hands who are not afraid of beasts and not afraid of Overseer Han. Your brother is the first-ranker of the Court. He is the obvious second. I went to him this morning." A pause. "He said he would come if you did."

Feng.

"And the third?"

"I had Zhao Yao in mind." She says it lightly. "He is fourteen, eighth layer, quiet, and trained in the Zhao house in the use of a spear. He is also, I understand, very good at carrying things." Her eyes rest on Jian's. "A leader should know her team."

She has already seen all of it.

He looks at the warrant. Four names. A mission worth a hundred and twenty points, a Rank 2 beast, a Level 2 root. The one thing he wants, in a hand that wants it too.

"The marrow," he says.

"Yes."

"Leader's right."

"Leader's right." Tan Ruyan does not blink. "I have been honest with you since the board. I mean to have it. I mean to have the root, too, as much as Han will give. I will not apologize for it, any more than you would apologize for the same." She closes the folder. "You may refuse. There are other teams. But I do not think you will find another with a first-ranker and a Pill Hall apprentice who reads fire."

She is offering me what I need, he thinks. And taking what I cannot afford.

It is, he realizes, the cleverest thing anyone has done to him since he came to the Sect.

* * *

The warrant requires a bond.

It is a plain rule and a hard one. Every member of a mission team deposits eighty points with the Contribution Hall for the length of the expedition. If the team returns, the bond is paid back with the reward. If a member dies or deserts, the points are forfeit to the Hall. The Sect does not lend its beasts and its herbs to children who may not return.

Jian has ninety.

He stands at the counter of the new Deacon with the slip in his hand. The heavy honest face looks down at him, and a brush goes across the register in a plain brown ink.

Lin Jian, Outer Sect 0417. Bond, mission warrant 114: eighty points. Balance: ten.

He had not expected it to hurt. It is only a number. But he has carried the number for a month, through the Terrace Nine baskets and the Pill Hall sweeps and the nights of Marrow Wash, and it was the first thing in the Sect that was entirely his. Ten is not enough to buy a meal on the credit he still owes.

Ten points, eleven stones.

He folds the slip into his sleeve.

"The Pill Hall will want its writ," says a dry voice at his shoulder.

He turns. Steward Gu stands there in his burn-scarred sleeves, with a folded paper held out between two stubby fingers. "The Elder wrote it last night," he says to the paper. "He did not say what for. He said that an apprentice who is going to the Medicine Valley will need a thing that says he is permitted to touch a root."

Jian takes it. It is a sheet of heavy cream paper, and it reads, in Bai's fast loose hand:

The bearer, Lin Jian, apprentice of the Pill Hall, is permitted to handle Level 2 herbs under the supervision of the Hall's seal. His handling is the Hall's responsibility. Bai.

There is a plum-colored seal at the bottom, and below the seal, in smaller letters, a single line.

I do not usually sign things. Do not make me regret it.

"He has said that before," says Gu to his hands, "to a Grand Elder's cook."

* * *

He tells Feng that night, in the dead yard, in the snow.

His brother has been told by Tan Ruyan, but he has not been told why. He stands against the fence with his arms folded and a pale clean light on his face from the stars, and listens with his head tilted, like a man listening for a sound in another room.

"I am not going for the points," says Feng.

"No."

"I am going because she asked, and because you said you would, and because the mission leaves in two days and I have been doing night duty on a stair that is no longer mine." A pause. "I am going because I do not like the way you said the root."

"How did I say it?"

"As if it were a word with a hole in it."

Jian looks down at the stick in his hand.

He knows. He has known for weeks. There is no purpose in lying to his brother about the shape of the thing. There is every purpose in lying about its contents.

"There is a pill," he says. "A true one. The Foundation Establishment, not the public one. The recipe was cut from the Pill Hall's scroll. I found part of it." That is true. It is also the only part that he can afford. "It needs five reagents. Two are locked behind Inner Sect rank. The root and the marrow are on this mission. The jade powder is at the auction, on the fifteenth."

"Where did you find the recipe?"

"In the Pill Hall."

"Where, in the Pill Hall?"

"I will not tell you, Feng."

His brother is quiet for a long moment.

"That is honest," he says, finally. "I will take it." He pushes off the fence. "I need the pill, too. You know that. The public one is a coin flip. I have tried eleven times in the chambers, and I have bled on every floor in the Annex." His voice is dry and a little rough. "If there is a true one, I want to be standing next to it when it is made."

"It is not for you."

"I did not say it was."

"It is for me," says Jian. "Because of my roots. A five-element body cannot take the public pill at all. It would not survive the breakthrough." He lets his breath out. "I am sorry. I cannot give it to you."

"I know." Feng's smile is thin. "I am not asking you to. I am asking you to let me stand beside you while you find it. It is not the same."

Jian looks at him. The lantern is gone; the starlight is thin and cold; his brother's face is all bone and shadow. He thinks of the stairs at the Register, and the leg that went at the fourth breath, and the lock that hummed. He thinks of the lie he told in Willow Bend, and the one he told at the ford.

I am going to have to give him something.

"After," he says, slowly, "if there is any left."

"If there is any left." Feng nods. "Thank you."

"For what?"

"For not saying no." He turns to go, and over his shoulder, in the tone he used at the courtyard of Green Pine Hill: "You have been telling me no for six months. It was very restful to hear something else."

* * *

Zhao Yao receives his warrant in silence.

He takes it from the clerk in both hands. He reads his name on the second line, and the date, and the word spearman. His face does not change. But he looks up, once, across the crowded mission hall, and finds Jian by the wall, and for the length of a breath the two of them look at each other over the heads of three hundred people with an understanding too small to say aloud.

Ears, thinks Jian. And hands.

He nods. Zhao Yao inclines his head, a hair's breadth, and turns away to the clerk.

The mission hall noise rolls on. Tan Ruyan is talking to Wei Chen in a low steady voice, her folder open on the table between them. Wei Chen is nodding. Outside the open doors, snow is falling on the Hundred Stairs in great soft flakes. Somewhere far above, in the white haze, a new post is being cut for the fortieth landing, and the sound of the chisel comes down the mountain like a bird tapping on glass.

Twenty-three days.

He has a warrant, a writ, a bond, and a leader who wants what he wants. He has a brother who asks no questions and a spy who has none left to ask. He has no scan, no panel, no blade. He has a pangolin in a bag that is going to have to walk past a Medicine Valley gate under the eyes of a Level 2 herb warden, and a reason that he cannot give.

Tell them it is a pill.

He pushes off the wall and goes out into the snow.

* * *

Bai finds him in the herb store that night, among the dried roots, and hands him a bundle wrapped in a clean cloth.

"Bone," says the Elder. "Not iron. Tongs, a spade, a knife. Old stag-horn, worked in the Hall. I made them forty years ago for a Level 2 harvest I never got to attend." He sets the bundle on a crate and does not look at it. "They are yours to carry. You will bring them back."

Jian unwraps it. The tongs are the length of a forearm, pale and smooth, with joints of brass. The spade is a flat blade the size of his palm. The knife is thin and curved and sharp as a thorn. They are beautifully made, and they have not been used.

"Thank you, Elder."

"Do not thank me. I am hoping you will come back with a root." He eats a plum, thoughtfully. "A man with a pill on a shelf for fifty-two years learns to hope for strange things." The pale eyes rest on him. "The writ is the Hall's. The root, if it comes, is yours. If anything goes wrong, you will say that I sent you for the Hall."

"Yes, Elder."

"You will not say you went for yourself."

"No, Elder."

"Good." Bai nods. "Then I have done what an old man can. Go with whatever luck there is."

He leaves. Jian wraps the bone tools and puts them in his satchel next to the bag of dried plum. He sits among the roots for a time, in the dark and the smell of earth, with a pangolin shifting restlessly at his side.

Eighty points. A bond. A leader who wants what I want. A valley that has gone quiet.

He does not like the quiet.

* * *

The letter from home reaches him on the last evening.

It comes by the Outer Affairs courier, a thin bundle wrapped in oiled cloth, and a servant boy drops it on his cot with the careless speed of a person who has delivered four hundred. There are two pages. The first is in his father's firm square hand.

Jian. I have your request. I have read it three times. I have also read the Court's notice about the Deacon, and I will say only that I am glad you are alive. Your mother and I have spoken of the Zhao child. She says that a house which cannot shelter a seven-year-old is not worth the name of a house. I say that a house which shelters the nephew of the man who burned its granary is a house that will hear about it for the rest of its life. We are agreed on both. We will bring him, if he can be reached. We will say that he is a ward of the Court, placed with us by the Arbiter. It is a lie, but a small one, and I have told larger.

Do not tell the boy until it is done. A hope that fails is cruel.

Your father.

The second page is in a child's careful print, with the letters leaning slightly to the left.

Dear Jian. You wrote that the number was three. I counted the nice ones in the clan and it is four, not three. You forgot Mama. I know you do not count family but I do. Hu says he is making you something. He will not say what. It has a spring in it. Yue.

He reads it twice. A loose tight feeling rises in his throat, and he swallows it.

Four. She is right. He did forget.

Do not tell the boy until it is done.

He folds the pages. He does not, in the end, tell Zhao Yao. He will tell him when the child is on the road. But he finds the boy at the pump in the dark, and stops beside him, and says, as lightly as he can, "I have written to my father."

Zhao Yao stops with his hand on the handle. He does not look round.

"And?"

"He has read it three times."

It is the whole of the news, and it is the most that can be said. The boy at the pump stands very still. Then he nods, slowly, twice, and goes on working the handle, and does not speak again.

* * *

The Medicine Valley gate is a squat arch of black stone at the bottom of the northern cleft, with two Outer Affairs guards in blue and a bronze bell hung from the keystone. It is the hour before dawn. The sky is still violet. The snow lies a hand deep on the road, unbroken but for the marks of a single cart.

They assemble under the arch in the cold.

Tan Ruyan is first, in a plain gray cloak, with a spear of white ash across her shoulder and a satchel of silver-stitched leather at her hip. She stands with the straight easy poise of someone who has been in a hundred rooms and expects to be in a hundred more. Zhao Yao arrives second, with a spear of his own and a pack too big for him. Feng arrives third, in his old cloak, with a sword of plain iron strapped to his back and his limp barely visible.

Jian arrives last, with a satchel, a stick, and a beast bag under his tunic that he is carefully not touching.

Overseer Han waits on the arch's far side with his abacus at his belt and his bamboo pointer in his hand. He looks the party over once, from boots to hats. He is not a man who smiles at the start of anything.

"Four," he says.

"Four, Overseer," says Wei Chen, from beside him. The Inner Sect disciple has put on a long indigo cloak and a hood, and he carries nothing but a flat bamboo case at his hip. "I shall accompany the party as far as Terrace Eleven. After that the leader decides."

"I know the rule." Han taps the pointer on his palm. "Listen. I will say this once."

They listen.

"The terrace is guarded by an array. Opens at dawn, closes at dusk. Anyone inside at closing is inside until morning, and I will not come for you." The pointer ticks. "The roots are fist-sized. They sit one handspan beneath the soil. The leader breaks the earth. A Pill Hall hand draws the root. Nobody touches it with iron." His eyes find Jian. "Not a nail. Not a ring. A root of Earthheart that has touched iron is a root that has gone to rot."

"Yes, Overseer."

"You take two. Not three. Two. I have counted the plants, and I know how many are there. If I count one fewer, I will know." The pointer stops. "After the terrace, the team passes through the upper valley to the Beast Mountains edge. A boar herd has come down this season, where it has no business. Do not engage the old male. Do not engage a sow with young. The leader will choose which to cull." A pause. "I have lost three hunters this year. I should prefer to lose none."

Three.

He doesn't say it. But he looks at Jian when he says it, and Jian understands that the Overseer is not talking about hunters.

"Are there questions?" says Han.

"One, Overseer." It is Tan Ruyan. She has not moved. "The upper valley. Is it clear?"

The pointer goes still.

"Why do you ask?"

"The guard at the gate said the night-frogs were silent." She looks at the road. "I was told that the valley rings with them in the winter. It is the one sound everyone mentions."

The Overseer is quiet for a long moment. The wind moves in the pines beyond the arch. Under his cloak, Jian feels the beast bag tighten against his ribs as the creature inside stirs.

Silence, comes the thin warning along the bond. No small things. No wings. No water-things. Nothing.

Nothing?

Gone.

"The valley," says Han, slowly, "has been quiet for nine days." He lowers the pointer. "The deer have gone. The foxes. The night-frogs, the marsh-deer, the rock lizards. Even the crows. The beasts of the lower valley have been going up into the mountain for a week and a half, and none have come down." His red face is unreadable. "I do not know why. I have written to the Hall. They tell me it is the snow."

"Is it?"

"I have kept this valley thirty years," says the Overseer. "I have seen snow."

He turns his back on them and walks away under the arch, a short stout shape in a brown cloak, and the guards open the gate.

The iron groans. Beyond the arch, the road runs on between black pines into the blue gloom of the valley, and the snow on it is untouched. Not a hare's track. Not a bird's. Wei Chen draws his hood forward. Feng shifts his sword. Tan Ruyan, at the head of the party, lifts her white spear from her shoulder and holds it low, in both hands, as one carries a thing across a stream.

Nobody says anything. They go in.
